info.title: Sparky — Kea Energy's Home Energy Advisor
info.description: Every number in every answer is computed by Python and verified before it reaches the customer. The model writes the sentence; it never does the maths.

post.description:
Demo sign-in. See app/auth.py — this is not authentication.

503 rather than 404 when the flag is off, because "this deployment does not offer
demo logins" and "that email does not exist" are different answers and only one of
them should ever be true in front of a real customer.

get.description:
Every sign-in, passwords included, so the team can pick a scenario to test.

This endpoint hands out credentials. It is behind the same flag as the login itself
and returns 503 when that flag is off — the accounts are entirely synthetic, but an
endpoint that lists passwords should never be reachable by accident.

schema.title: Response Demo Accounts Api Auth Demo Accounts Get
Response Demo Session Api Auth Session Get
Response List Households Api Households Get

get.description: Return this household's dated usage without guessing missing days or bands.
Serve the published catalogue and only the plan fields known for this account.
Return exact annual demand or a labelled estimate from available account usage.

Billing data already held by the account repository, shaped for clients.

Database-backed accounts receive their actual current/prior bill facts. Fixture
accounts have no invoice ledger, so the endpoint returns the backend's own usage-cost
estimate as Pending rather than inventing due dates, payments or card details.

The signed-in customer's own details.

Reads the same `AccountContext` every other answer is built from, so the profile
screen and the assistant cannot disagree about who the customer is. Fields the
account does not carry come back null and the screen says "Not on file" — the
seeded households have no address or plan, and inventing one would be showing
somebody a fact about themselves that no record holds.

post.description:
Read an electricity bill from a photo or PDF and price it against Kea.

Open to a bill from any retailer — the point is somebody holding a bill from
somewhere else, asking whether they would be better off here.

**The reading and the recommendation are separated on purpose.** `bills/reader.py`
gets numbers off the page and knows nothing about Kea; `bills/compare.py` does
arithmetic on those numbers and never calls a model. The response carries both, so
the client can show the customer what was read *before* anything is concluded from
it — they are holding the bill, and they are the cheapest validator available.

Nothing is stored. The bytes are read, sent once, and dropped: a photographed bill
carries a name, an address and an account number, and this endpoint has no reason to
be the place any of that comes to rest.

get.description:
The bill-shock warning. A GET, because it has to reach the customer unprompted.

Every other endpoint answers a question somebody asked. A warning that only appears
if you think to ask for it is not a warning, so this is polled by the dashboard
rather than routed through chat.

`as_at_day` truncates the cycle so the warning can be seen mid-cycle. Each seeded
household holds a complete July, and a warning delivered on day 31 is not a warning,
it is a bill.

Which days show what is not obvious from the data:

* **H-COLD is the demo household.** It is the only one whose usage actually tracks
  the HDD series, so it is the only one that reaches the weather-normalised path and
  produces a cause breakdown ("$41 of this is the cold snap"). Read it around day 14.
* **H-JUL always falls back to the straight line.** Its daily totals are real measured
  data and `_HDD_JULY` is an invented series built for H-COLD, so the two do not
  correspond and the regression correctly refuses to fit. That is the honest state of
  the fixture data — manufacturing a correlated weather series for it would be
  inventing the exact kind of figure this product exists to prevent. The response says
  `method: straight_line` and the narration is forbidden from attributing anything to
  temperature.

Reads through the repository (KEA-33) rather than `fixtures` directly. The warning
and the dashboard summary quote the same dollar figure, so they have to come from
the same source — a warning served from a Python file while `/households` serves
from PostgreSQL is two numbers that disagree in front of a judge.

What this household asked to be told about, and how.

Returns defaults for a customer who has never opened Settings rather than 404. There
is no such thing as a household with no alerting behaviour — there is only one whose
behaviour nobody has changed, and the screen has to render either way.

put.description:
Set the thresholds.

The path parameter wins over the body. A body carrying a different `account_ref` is a
request to write one customer's settings under another's id, and it is the shape a
broken client produces long before it is the shape an attacker does — either way the
only safe reading is the one in the URL.

Validation (monotonic ladder, 5-200% bounds, real timezone) happens in the Pydantic
model, so an invalid ladder is a 422 with a readable message rather than a policy
layer quietly sorting the numbers behind the customer's back.

get.description:
What this household has told us about their home.

Returns an empty context for a household that has never been asked, rather than 404 —
"nothing known" is a real state and the app has to render it.

post.description:
Record an answer to a clarifying question.

The answer is a closed set — yes, no, not sure — plus at most a date and a count.
Deliberately not free text: taking prose back and pasting it into the next prompt
would put uncomputed figures into the model's context ("probably 400 kWh"), which is
the exact failure the FactBundle exists to prevent. See `app/clarify/schemas.py`.

A 404 for an unknown question id rather than silently recording it: an id we do not
recognise means the client is out of date, and storing it would mark a question as
asked that this backend has no way to ask again.

get.description:
Where this household's power goes, split by behaviour rather than by appliance.

A GET on the household rather than a chat-only tool, because it is the same figure the
dashboard draws and the assistant quotes — and two surfaces computing it separately is
how they start to disagree. Everything here comes out of
`app/analytics/disaggregation.py`; this handler computes nothing.

`available: false` with a reason is a real response and the frontend must render it.
An account with no half-hourly data cannot have its standing load separated, and the
honest screen says so rather than showing a chart with one slice in it.

Which platforms can be connected, and which of them are actually credentialled.

`False` means the connector exists but has no client id, so the connect screen greys it
out rather than offering a button that dead-ends. HomeKit reads True with no
credential and that is correct — there is nothing for this backend to hold, because the
iOS app reads HomeKit on the phone and posts daily totals.

schema.title: Response Homelink Providers Api Homelink Providers Get

post.description:
Scan the local network for smart devices that announce themselves.

A POST rather than a GET despite reading nothing, because it is not free and not
cacheable: it puts multicast traffic on the API server's network and takes seconds. A GET
invites a browser, a proxy or a dashboard poll to repeat it, and a discovery scan that
runs on every page load is a scan running without anybody asking.

Only ever runs when somebody asks. Nothing is stored — the result goes back to the
caller and is dropped. See `app/homelink/discovery.py` on why that matters more here
than anywhere else in this service.

schema.title: Response Homelink Discover Api Homelink Discover Post

put.description: Restore a typed, on-device EV answer into this household's server context.

Candidate device models for a future offline release, not live downloads.

The mobile app currently records interest only. Distribution sizes must be
verified against shipped artefacts before any download is offered.

get.description:
Everything a device needs to answer this household's questions with no network.

Fetched by the client while it still has a connection, on the customer's schedule —
the server never pushes. Carries pre-computed fact bundles, not meter readings: a
device holding the raw series is a device whose on-device model can be asked to add
it up, which is the one thing this architecture exists to prevent, on the platform
where it is hardest to audit.

See `app/offline.py` and `docs/adr/0008-offline-first-narration.md`.

post.description: Non-streaming path. Simpler to test; /chat/stream is what the apps use.

SSE. Streams the answer as the assistant works.

The event sequence is documented on `pipeline.answer_stream`, which produces it.
Six names, and `reset` is the one worth reading about before writing a client.

`chart` is the newest and the only optional one: when a lookup returns something
chartable, its own figures are emitted as `{kind, title, unit, points, caveat,
source}` so a client can draw the answer as well as print it. At most one arrives
per turn and most turns have none, so a client that ignores the event is still
correct — it just shows prose where another client shows prose and a picture.

**What changed here, and why the old comment above this function no longer applies.**
It used to say verification is a whole-text check, so the answer had to be generated
in full and checked before a single token could be streamed. That constraint came
from the number-checker, which compared the finished prose against a pre-computed
fact bundle. There is no bundle now — the model reads the data itself and its
figures are traceable to the tool results recorded alongside the answer — so nothing
has to be withheld until the last sentence lands. The stream is live again, which is
most of the perceived speed.

Vapi Custom LLM endpoint. Same agent, OpenAI wire format.

Vapi places an outbound call (Tier 3 bill-shock alert), handles STT/TTS, and
sends us an OpenAI-shaped request with the customer's transcribed speech. We
run it through the same `answer()` path every other channel uses and return the
result as OpenAI-compatible SSE chunks.

Errors are spoken apologies, not HTTP status codes. A 404 on a phone call is
silence — the customer hears nothing. The apology is the error handling.

**Escalation no longer short-circuits the answer.** The old version returned a
transfer line and hung up on the explanation, because layer 0 decided a call was a
hardship call from keywords before anything had been read. The agent decides while
holding the account, and an escalation is a thing it does *alongside* answering —
somebody in payment difficulty who asked why the bill went up should be told why,
warmly, and then put through. `result.escalate` is logged so the Vapi assistant's
own transfer rule can act on it.

enabled.title: Enabled
enabled.description: Master switch. False means no bill-shock alerting at all on any channel — the assessment is still computed and still visible in the app, because turning off the interruption is not the same as turning off the product.

tier1_pct.title: Tier1 Pct
tier1_pct.description: Percent over expectation at which an email goes out.

tier2_pct.title: Tier2 Pct
tier2_pct.description: Percent over expectation at which a text message goes out.

tier3_pct.title: Tier3 Pct
tier3_pct.description: Percent over expectation at which the assistant calls them.

min_overshoot_nzd.title: Min Overshoot Nzd
min_overshoot_nzd.description: Dollar floor under every tier. A percentage alone fires constantly on small bills — 20% over on a $40 cycle is $8, which nobody wants a text about.

voice_enabled.title: Voice Enabled
voice_enabled.description: Opt-IN, unlike the other two. An automated call is the most intrusive thing this product can do and the one most easily mistaken for a scam, so it is off until the customer asks for it.

quiet_hours_start.title: Quiet Hours Start
quiet_hours_start.description: Local hour after which the phone is off limits.

quiet_hours_end.title: Quiet Hours End
quiet_hours_end.description: Local hour at which it is fair game again.

offline_model_opt_in.title: Offline Model Opt In
offline_model_opt_in.description: The customer asked for an on-device model because their connection is unreliable. Lives here rather than in a separate table because it is the same shape of thing — a per-customer choice about how the product reaches them — and because the mobile app fetches both in one request on launch.

bill_reminders.title: Bill Reminders
bill_reminders.description: Send a reminder before a bill falls due. Same shape as the flag above and here for the same reason: it is a per-customer choice about being contacted. It sat in React state until now, so the Settings screen offered a switch the alerting engine never heard — the customer turned reminders off, the toggle moved, and nothing else in the system changed.

theme.title: Theme
theme.description: Light or dark. Appearance rather than contact, but stored per customer because a preference kept only in `localStorage` is one they have to set again on every device and lose whenever the browser is cleared. The client still writes localStorage first so the theme applies before this request returns — the stored value is what a second device reads.

AlertPreferences.title: AlertPreferences
AlertPreferences.description:
One household's alerting settings. Pydantic rather than a dataclass because this
crosses the API boundary in both directions and the validation below is the whole
point — a threshold ladder that is not monotonic is not a coherent instruction, and
it must be rejected at the edge rather than sorted out in the policy layer.

tier.title: Tier
tier.description: 1 email · 2 sms · 3 voice. 0 when nothing triggered.

channels.title: Channels
channels.description: Every channel this tier calls for, lowest first.

deferred.title: Deferred
deferred.description: Eligible, but held until the customer's quiet hours end.

confidence.title: Confidence
confidence.description: P(the cycle lands above the threshold this tier fired at), 0-1. Shown next to the warning because it is the honest answer to 'how sure are you' — and because the tier ladder now escalates on confidence as well as severity.

destination.title: Destination
destination.description: Where tier 1 landed — an .eml path under the file backend.

already_sent.title: Already Sent
already_sent.description: True when this cycle and tier were already alerted. The dashboard polls, so this is the normal steady state, not an error.

AlertSummary.title: AlertSummary
AlertSummary.description:
What the warning escalated to, reported alongside the warning itself.

On the response rather than behind its own endpoint because the UI has to show the
tier next to the figures that produced it, and a second request could return a
different assessment.

`sent` is what actually went out — today only `email` can appear in it. `channels`
is what the tier calls for, so the UI can show the full ladder with the
not-yet-wired rungs greyed rather than pretending tier 3 does not exist.

AnnualDemandSummary.title: AnnualDemandSummary
AnnualDemandSummary.description: Exact annual demand or a labelled estimate from available account usage.

BillAnalysis.title: BillAnalysis
BillAnalysis.description:
A photographed bill, read and priced against Kea.

Two objects rather than one flattened result, because they have different standings
and the client must be able to show that. `reading` is what a model saw on a
photograph — checkable by the person holding it, and wrong in ways our own data
never is. `comparison` is arithmetic over those numbers, and is exactly as reliable
as they are.

Left as free-form dicts on purpose: the shapes are defined and documented by
`app/bills/`, and restating them here as Pydantic models would be a second
definition to keep in step for no gain — nothing in this service validates against
them, and the client renders whichever fields are non-null.

reasons.title: Reasons
reasons.description: above_expectation | colder_than_normal | higher_daily_use. Empty when nothing triggered.

days_remaining.title: Days Remaining
days_remaining.description: What makes this actionable rather than just bad news.

expected_cost_nzd.title: Expected Cost Nzd
expected_cost_nzd.description: What this customer would not be surprised by. See `expectation_basis`.

expectation_basis.title: Expectation Basis
expectation_basis.description: own_same_period_last_year | own_recent_cycles | comparable_homes. The honesty control for the whole feature: only the first two license 'more than you usually pay'. The seeded demo households are on the third, and the UI must word the comparison accordingly.

recent_trend_pct.title: Recent Trend Pct
recent_trend_pct.description: Opening third of the cycle against the closing third. Shown beside the usage chart. Deliberately NOT a trigger: a rising trend says the cycle is getting worse, not that it is already expensive.

thresholds_pct.title: Thresholds Pct
thresholds_pct.description: The customer's own tier thresholds, echoed so the UI can show the warning against the level they set rather than a hard-coded one.

tier_probabilities.title: Tier Probabilities
tier_probabilities.description: P(the cycle clears each tier's threshold), 0-1, keyed by tier.

facts.title: Facts
facts.description: The same computed facts the narration is limited to, so the UI and the assistant can never disagree about a figure.

question.description: A clarifying question, when layer 1 found a quantified gap it cannot close on its own — an unexplained step in everyday load, or a weather fit that would not converge. Null is the common case and the correct default: a household whose bill is fully explained has nothing to be asked. Answer it at POST /households/{id}/context/answers. See app/clarify/ for how it is chosen.

alert.description: What was escalated, if anything. Null when the warning did not trigger.

BillShockWarning.title: BillShockWarning
BillShockWarning.description:
The proactive half of the product.

Everything else in this API answers a question the customer asked. This one has to
reach them *before* the bill does, so it is a GET the dashboard polls rather than a
chat intent — a warning that only appears if you think to ask for it is not a
warning.

`triggered` is the only field the UI should branch on. The figures are present either
way so the dashboard can show a calm "on track" state without a second request.

dominant.title: Dominant
dominant.description: weather | behaviour | everyday_load, or null when no single cause accounts for at least 35% of the overshoot. Null is a real answer: '31/34/35' is a pie chart pretending to be advice.

CauseBreakdown.title: CauseBreakdown
CauseBreakdown.description:
Where the overshoot came from, in dollars that sum to it exactly.

`explained` false means the weather regression was not usable and the whole overshoot
sits in `everyday_load_nzd` unattributed. The UI must not draw a cause chart in that
state — an unexplained overshoot shown with a confident breakdown is worse than one
shown with none.

conversation_id.title: Conversation Id
conversation_id.description: Continue an existing conversation. Omit on the first message; send back whatever the previous response returned. Ignored when persistence is off, and ignored if it belongs to a different customer.

sources.title: Sources
sources.description: Every lookup behind this answer, in the order it was made.

escalate_to_human.title: Escalate To Human
escalate_to_human.description: A support concern was recorded or direct contact advised; no staff delivery is implied.

escalation_reason.title: Escalation Reason
escalation_reason.description: Why, in the assistant's own words. Null unless `escalate_to_human`. The The UI should explain how to contact verified support; this string is for the transcript and concern record.

conversation_id.title: Conversation Id
conversation_id.description: Send this back on the next message to keep the thread together. Null when persistence is off — there is no conversation to continue.

tier.title: Tier
tier.description: Who handled this turn. 1 the assistant alone, 2 the assistant with a Kea agent watching and able to step in, 3 a person only — the assistant acknowledges and stops. Decided in Python from the message and the account on every channel, never by the model; see app/hardship/. The model can raise it by calling handoff_to_human and can never lower it.

tier_reason.title: Tier Reason
tier_reason.description: Why this tier, in words a support lead would use.

emotion.title: Emotion
emotion.description: How the customer's message read: frustration, anxiety, confusion, distrust, shame, resignation, urgency or gratitude. Null when nothing was detected, which is the common case. It changed how the reply was WRITTEN and nothing else — it is not a tier input and carries no score; see app/hardship/emotions.py. Intended for the agent console, not for showing back to the customer: telling somebody 'we detected that you are frustrated' is worse than simply answering them properly.

emotion_intensity.title: Emotion Intensity
emotion_intensity.description: mild | moderate | strong. Null whenever `emotion` is.

id.title: Id
id.description: Stable. Used to record that it was asked and answered.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.description: The question as the customer reads it. Composed by Python, not the model — a model that writes its own questions is a model choosing what to ask about somebody's home.

ClarifyingQuestion.title: ClarifyingQuestion
ClarifyingQuestion.description: One question, and the arithmetic that justifies asking it.

Confidence.title: Confidence
Confidence.description:
How much this figure can carry, and therefore what may be said about it.

This is the field that makes the whole feature safe. A device that reports its own
energy meter is a measurement; a device that reports on/off and has a nameplate rating
is an estimate; a device inferred from a schedule is a guess. Presenting all three as
"your heat pump used 4.2 kWh" would put the product's central claim behind the weakest
of them.

CustomerProfile.title: CustomerProfile
CustomerProfile.description:
Who the signed-in customer is, for the profile screen.

Every field below `customer_id` is optional, and the screen shows "Not on file"
rather than a placeholder for the ones that are missing. That is not defensive
coding — the seeded `public.*` households genuinely have no address or plan, and a
profile page that invented one would be showing somebody a detail about themselves
that nobody holds.

The page it replaces was hardcoded to "Adela Parkson", so every one of the sixteen
logins saw the same person's name, address and phone number.

DemoAccountCard.title: DemoAccountCard
DemoAccountCard.description:
A sign-in the credentials panel can offer. Includes the password, which is only
acceptable because every account behind it is synthetic — see app/auth.py.

DeviceClass.title: DeviceClass
DeviceClass.description:
What kind of load it is, in the only terms that matter for a power bill.

Deliberately coarse. A vendor taxonomy has two hundred device types and this has
eight, because the question the product answers is "where is the money going" and a
smart bulb and a smart plug on a lamp are the same answer. Precision we cannot use is
surface area we have to maintain.

device_id.title: Device Id
device_id.description: Stable per (provider, household). Never a serial.

label.title: Label
label.description: What the customer calls it — 'Lounge heat pump'.

runtime_minutes.title: Runtime Minutes
runtime_minutes.description: Minutes the device was drawing power.

energy_kwh.title: Energy Kwh
energy_kwh.description: Reported by the device's own meter, if it has one.

rated_watts.title: Rated Watts
rated_watts.description: Nameplate power. A maximum, not a draw.

DeviceObservation.title: DeviceObservation
DeviceObservation.description:
One device, one day. The atom of this package.

A day rather than an event because of the minimisation rule in the module docstring,
and because a bill is billed per day. Anything finer would be data we cannot use held
at a resolution we cannot justify.

reason.title: Reason
reason.description: Why there is no breakdown. Null when `available`. A real response the UI must render — an account with no half-hourly data cannot have its standing load separated, and the honest screen says so rather than drawing one slice.

heating_fit_r_squared.title: Heating Fit R Squared
heating_fit_r_squared.description: How much of daily variation the weather explains for this household. Null when heating was not broken out at all.

EnergyBreakdown.title: EnergyBreakdown
EnergyBreakdown.description:
Where a household's power goes. See app/analytics/disaggregation.py.

**This does not identify appliances**, and no surface rendering it may imply otherwise.
A whole-house meter reads one number for the whole house; the categories here are
behaviours that are each separately measurable, which is a different claim and the only
honest one available.

basis.title: Basis
basis.description: How this figure was arrived at, in one clause.

EnergyCategory.title: EnergyCategory
EnergyCategory.description:
One slice of the bill, split by behaviour rather than by appliance.

`confidence` is the field that decides how this may be presented, and the frontend has
to honour it as much as the assistant does. `measured` came off a meter. `fitted` came
off this household's own regression and is an estimate — a chart that renders it
identically to a measured slice is a chart that overstates what is known. `residual` is
what is left after the others, so it carries their error and must be labelled as
everything else rather than as a finding.

unit.title: Unit
unit.description: kWh | kWh/day | NZD | NZD/year | % | x | days

label.title: Label
label.description: human-readable name for the narrator's benefit

display.title: Display
display.description: pre-formatted string, e.g. '$290' or '2.4 kWh a day'

Fact.title: Fact
Fact.description:
One computed value. Every number the customer ever sees starts life here.

`display` is the canonical rendering. The narration prompt tells the model to
copy these strings verbatim rather than formatting numbers itself, which both
raises pass rate on small models and gives the verifier an exact string to match.

period.title: Period
period.description: human phrase for the window, e.g. 'July 2026'

caveats.title: Caveats
caveats.description: Claims the narrator must NOT make. Half-hourly data cannot identify an appliance, so 'do not name an appliance' belongs here on most bundles.

narration_limit.title: Narration Limit
narration_limit.description: How many facts the *model* is shown, when that should be fewer than the API returns. Null means all of them, which is the right default for every bundle small enough to narrate whole.

FactBundle.title: FactBundle
FactBundle.description:
Everything layer 2 is allowed to know, and nothing else.

Deliberately does NOT carry raw meter readings, name, address or account number.
Layer 1 computes; the model narrates. Keeping PII out of here is both the privacy
control and — once we move to a hosted model — the prompt-cache boundary.

detail.title: Detail
detail.description: The fitted relationship, or why the fit was not usable.

cost_p10_nzd.title: Cost P10 Nzd
cost_p10_nzd.description: Low end of the 80% prediction interval.

cost_p90_nzd.title: Cost P90 Nzd
cost_p90_nzd.description: High end of the 80% prediction interval.

confidence_width_pct.title: Confidence Width Pct
confidence_width_pct.description: Interval width as a percent of the point estimate. Narrows as the cycle progresses; this is what stops a phone call on day four.

base_load_kwh_per_day.title: Base Load Kwh Per Day
base_load_kwh_per_day.description: Fitted temperature-independent load. Null if not fitted.

heating_kwh_per_hdd.title: Heating Kwh Per Hdd
heating_kwh_per_hdd.description: Fitted kWh per heating degree day. Null if not fitted.

ForecastSummary.title: ForecastSummary
ForecastSummary.description:
How the projection was produced. On the response because a figure that does not
carry its method is a figure nobody can check — the weather-normalised and
straight-line projections disagree by real money on a cold cycle.

Gap.title: Gap
Gap.description: What we could not work out. One per question the catalogue can ask.

HouseholdContext.title: HouseholdContext
HouseholdContext.description:
What the customer has told us about their home, as typed facts.

Fed back into layer 1, never into the prompt. A confirmed new appliance since a date
lets the attribution *name* the step it already found rather than leaving it in the
unexplained bucket — and that is the entire payoff of asking.

Every field is nullable and null means "never asked", which is deliberately different
from `False` meaning "asked and denied". See the module docstring.

HouseholdSummary.title: HouseholdSummary
HouseholdSummary.description: Shape the frontend charts against. Fixture-backed until Day 2.

HouseholdUsageSeries.title: HouseholdUsageSeries
HouseholdUsageSeries.description: Dated usage for a requested range; never fills missing days or bands.

Hypothesis.title: Hypothesis
Hypothesis.description:
What a question is testing. One per thing a household can tell us that changes the
arithmetic.

Intent.title: Intent
Intent.description:
A closed set of pre-computable questions. **Offline and bill-shock only now.**

This was the spine of the request path: a keyword router mapped free text onto one
of these, and the intent chose the analytics, the prompt and the caveats. It no
longer does — the agent reads the question and the data, and nothing classifies a
customer's message into a bucket before it is understood. See `app/pipeline.py`.

Two things still use it, both legitimately:

* `app/offline.py` pre-computes a pack of answers for a device with no connection.
  It has to guess what will be asked, so a fixed list is the only option available.
* `app/analytics/billshock.py` labels a proactive warning, which nobody asked a
  question to receive.

Neither is a classifier over customer text.

## Two families, and why the second one exists

The **usage** intents below the divider are the original ten: they all answer a
question about consumption, and every one of them needs analytics to run first.

The **account** intents are facts about the customer's own account — balance, plan,
rates, connection, payment method. They were unroutable before, which meant "what
plan am I on?" and "when is my bill due?" returned `OUT_OF_SCOPE`. That is a bad
answer to a question the service can answer perfectly from one mart row, and it is
a large share of what a real energy assistant is asked.

They are a separate family rather than more of the same because the layer-3
contract differs: an account fact is a *lookup*, so its bundle is a copy of stored
values rather than the output of a computation. Nothing is derived, so nothing can
be derived wrongly.

LoginResponse.title: LoginResponse
LoginResponse.description:
Who signed in, and which household to show them.

The token is temporary and valid only for synthetic demo accounts. It authorizes
new household write paths, not real customer access.

limitation.title: Limitation
limitation.default: Plan switches are not available in the mobile API. Contact Customer Care to change plans.

OfflineAnswer.title: OfflineAnswer
OfflineAnswer.description: One precomputed intent, ready for the device to narrate.

OfflineModelOption.title: OfflineModelOption
OfflineModelOption.description:
One candidate on-device model; this build does not distribute it.

Sizes are the quantised download, not the parameter count, because that is the number
the customer is agreeing to spend. Quoting "1B parameters" to somebody deciding
whether to use their data is not an answer to the question they asked.

schema_version.title: Schema Version
schema_version.description: Bumped when the pack's shape changes. A device on an older app must refuse a pack it does not understand rather than reading fields positionally — the failure mode otherwise is a stale answer with confident wrong numbers.

OfflinePack.title: OfflinePack
OfflinePack.description:
Everything a device needs to answer without a network.

Carries no raw meter series, and that is deliberate rather than a size optimisation.
A device holding `daily_kwh` is a device whose model can be asked to add it up, and
the first time someone wires the chat box straight to the readings "to make offline
smarter", the no-arithmetic guarantee is gone on the platform where it is hardest to
audit.

Provider.title: Provider
Provider.description:
Where the data came from. Carried on every observation because the trust level and
the legal basis differ per provider, and a mixed-provider household is normal.

since.title: Since
since.description: When it started, if they know. Optional and often absent — most people remember 'a few weeks ago', not a date, and a required field here would make them invent one.

count.title: Count
count.description: Extra people, for MORE_OCCUPANTS. Bounded because a typo should not become a household of 4,000.

arguments.title: Arguments
arguments.description: What it was asked for, when that narrows the result.

source.title: Source
source.description: The table or computation behind it, in words a customer can read.

ok.title: Ok
ok.description: False when the lookup failed or the data was not available for this account. Shown rather than hidden: 'I could not check that' is a different answer from 'I did not look', and only one of them is honest about a gap.

SourceRef.title: SourceRef
SourceRef.description:
One lookup the assistant made, for the transparency panel.

This replaced `facts` on the chat response. The two answer different questions and
the new one is the question customers were actually asking: `facts` listed the
figures Python computed *before* the model saw the message, which was the same list
for everyone who tripped the same keyword. This says what was consulted for *this*
answer and where each result came from — which is checkable, and is what makes
"every number traces to a source" a claim rather than a slogan.

_VapiCompletionRequest.title: _VapiCompletionRequest
_VapiCompletionRequest.description:
Vapi's OpenAI-compatible request shape.

Vapi sends this as its "Custom LLM" integration. We accept the full shape
and ignore everything except `messages` — the model choice is ours (layer 2),
and streaming is always on because Vapi expects chunked SSE.
